senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: the quality of moral purity
senses.comment: In a number of languages the meaning of ἁγνεία and ἁγνότης is expressed idiomatically, for example, to have a clean heart, to not have other thoughts, or to not cover up one’s real desires.

senses.def: to engage in an athletic contest, with emphasis upon competition

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being without a mixture of evil and hence to being pure
pertaining to a lack of capacity to reason or think properly
senses.comment: In rendering 2 Peter 2:12 one may translate ‘creatures unable to reason’ as ‘wild animals,’ for this is clearly the reference of the phrase ἄλογα ζῷα.

senses.def: pertaining to not providing a reason or cause, in view of something being contrary to reason
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of being unreasonable is being something which people should not think. Note that ἄλογος[b] refers to that which is contrary to proper reasoning, while ἄλογος[a] (30.12) pertains to a lack of capacity to reason.

senses.def: to become able to see, whether for the first time or again
to cause someone to become physically refreshed as the result of resting from work
senses.comment: In some languages it may be difficult to speak of ‘causing someone to become refreshed by resting.’ Normally this would be accomplished simply by causing a person not to have to work. Accordingly, Matthew 11:28 may be expressed in some languages as ‘I will make it possible for you no longer to have to work’ or ‘… to toil hard.’ This, however, must not be understood merely in the sense of ‘to give a person a vacation’ or ‘to make it possible for someone to live without working.’

senses.def: to become physically refreshed after ceasing activity or work
senses.comment: In the use of ἀναπαύομαι[a] and ἀνάπαυσις[b], the focus of meaning seems to be upon the restorative character of rest rather than mere cessation of activity (see 68.34).

senses.def: to remain in a place, with the implication of continuing to rest
to continue to be in a state in or on someone, with the implication of beneficent result
an adult male person of marriageable age
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ‘now that I am a man’ is ‘now that I am grown’ or ‘now that I have become strong.’

senses.def: a human being (normally an adult)
senses.comment: In Matthew 14:35 (ἐπιγνόντες αὐτὸν οἱ ἄνδρες τοῦ τόπου ἐκείνου ‘when the people of that place recognized him’) one may argue that οἱ ἄνδρες refers specifically to males, but the context would seem to indicate that the reference is to people in general. In translation a pronominal expression may frequently be employed when ἀνήρ[b] occurs in the text, for example, ‘when those who lived in that place recognized him.’|It is not uncommon in languages for a term which is often used to refer to an adult male to be employed also in a generic sense of ‘person.’ This is especially true when such terms are used in the plural form.|In a number of instances, generic meanings of receptor languages have not been recognized as such, since translators have assumed that such receptor-language terms refer only to members of a particular tribe or group (because they have been found only in specific contexts), while in reality such terms often designate people in general. One must, however, be on the alert for seemingly generic terms which refer only to the so-called ‘in-group,’ that is to say, members of a particular tribe, society, or community.|The parallelism in the Romans 4:8 quotation from indicates clearly that the reference of ἀνήρ is not a particular male but any person.

senses.def: a man who is married to a woman
senses.comment: ἀνήρ in the meaning of ‘husband’ is normally clearly marked by context, usually involving a so- called ‘possessive marker,’ though in some contexts such as John 4:17 and Matthew 19:10, the distinctions in meaning are quite clear, but it is only from each individual context that one can determine whether ἀνήρ means simply ‘man’ (see 9.24) or ‘husband.’ See also discussion at 10.54.

senses.def: a container or vessel, primarily for liquids or wet objects; perhaps made of leather, used for drawing water
the state of being someone in whom confidence cannot be placed
senses.comment: The occurrence of both ἀπιστία and πίστις (31.88) in this expression in Romans 3:3 may cause certain difficulties in appropriately rendering the meaning in other languages. It may therefore be necessary to spell out in some detail the fuller implications of ἀπιστία and πίστις. Moreover, the question implies a negative response, but the question (since it is rhetorical) can easily be rendered as a strong negative statement, for example, ‘the fact that they were persons who could not be trusted does not mean that God cannot be trusted.’

senses.def: to refuse to put one’s trust or reliance in something or someone
senses.comment: One of the serious problems involved in rendering ‘to believe’ or ‘to refuse to believe’ is that so frequently the NT text does not indicate precisely the goal or object of such belief.|In a number of languages, however, the syntactic requirements are such that some clear goal must be in the immediate context. For example, in Mark 16:16 it may be possible to translate ‘whoever refuses to believe the good news shall be condemned.’

senses.def: to not believe in the good news about Jesus Christ and hence not become a follower

senses.subdomain: Hold a Wrong View, Be Mistaken
senses.def: to cause someone to definitely go astray in one’s beliefs or views
glosses: to cause to have completely wrong views

senses.def: to no longer believe what is true, but to start believing what is false
senses.comment: Though in some languages one can preserve the figurative meaning of ‘to wander’ or ‘to go astray’ in connection with truth, it is not possible to do so in many languages, and therefore it may be necessary to spell out in some detail precisely what is involved, for example, ‘to stop believing what is true and to start believing what is false.’

senses.subdomain: Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With
senses.def: to cause someone to be pleased with someone or something
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to cause someone to be pleased with something’ is expressed as ‘to cause someone to be happy about’ or ‘to cause someone to feel good about.’

senses.def: pertaining to a fire that cannot be put out
senses.comment: It may be necessary in some languages to render ‘unquenchable’ by an active equivalent, for example, ‘a fire that no one can put out.’

senses.def: to cause something to be clearly evident
glosses: to cause to be clear to

senses.def: pertaining to not being useful
senses.comment: In a number of languages usefulness or lack of usefulness can only be expressed in terms of a verb meaning ‘to help,’ so that in Philemon 1:11 it may be necessary to translate ‘at one time he did not help you at all and now he can help both you and me.’

senses.def: pertaining to being without such qualities as deserve praise or commendation
the name of the Devil as the prince of the demons
the father of Balaam
senses.comment: Βοσόρ is the reading in most NT manuscripts for Βεώρ (); see 93.74. Βοσύρ is an incidental variant spelling (2 Peter 2:15, apparatus)

senses.subdomain: Regions Below the Surface of the Earth
senses.def: a place of punishment for the dead
senses.comment: The Greek term γέεννα is derived from a Hebrew phrase meaning ‘Valley of Hinnom,’ a ravine running along the south side of Jerusalem and a place where the rubbish from the city was constantly being burned. According to late Jewish popular belief, the last judgment was to take place in this valley, and hence the figurative extension of meaning from ‘Valley of Hinnom’ to ‘hell.’ In most languages γέεννα is rendered as ‘place of punishment’ or ‘place where the dead suffer’ or ‘place where the dead suffer because of their sins.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to control oneself by thorough discipline
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to discipline oneself’ is literally ‘to make oneself obey.’ This may sometimes be expressed idiomatically as ‘to command one’s heart.’

senses.def: to experience vigorous training and control, with the implication of increased physical and/or moral strength
senses.comment: In rendering γυμνάζω in Hebrews 12:11 it may be important in some languages to translate ‘those who have learned by such punishment’ or ‘those whose ways have been made right by such punishment’ or ‘those who because of punishment have learned how they must act.’

senses.def: (derivative of Δέρβη ‘Derbe,’ 93.462) a person who lives in or is a native of Derbe
to engage in some relatively detailed discussion of a matter
to provide instruction in a formal or informal setting
senses.comment: The equivalent of ‘to teach’ in many languages is simply a causative form of a verb meaning ‘to learn’ or ‘to know,’ for example, ‘to cause to learn’ or ‘to cause to know.’ In choosing a term for ‘to teach’ it is important to avoid an expression which will denote merely classroom activity.

senses.def: (derivative of διδάσκω ‘to teach,’ 33.224) the content of what is taught
to regard something as presumably true, but without particular certainty
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ‘to suppose’ or ‘to presume’ is ‘to think somewhat’ or ‘to think perhaps’ or ‘to think a little.’ In some instances the lack of certainty is spelled out clearly as ‘to think, but not with certainty’ or ‘to think, but not to know’ or ‘to think, but not to be sure.’

senses.def: to be disposed to some desire or intent
senses.comment: For another interpretation of δοκέω in 1 Corinthians 11:16, see 30.96.

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: to make a choice on the basis of something being better or superior
senses.comment: It would also be possible to translate the ‘if’ clause in 1 Corinthians 11:16 as ‘if anyone is disposed to be contentious’ or ‘if anyone wants to quarrel about it’ (see δοκέω[b], 25.7).

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: those who have a reputation of being important or are generally recognized as being important
to hold an opinion based upon appearances which may be significantly different from reality
to allow someone to do something
(an idiom, literally: to leave off until) to cease from what one is doing, with the implication of strong admonition
an emphatic marker of condition
purposely to avoid association with someone
glosses: to have nothing to do with

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἐκκλίνω[a] ‘to avoid,’ 34.41) to no longer put one’s trust or confidence in someone
to cease doing something, with the implication of engaging in some alternative
to possess too little of some substance
(two different forms of the same base, compare 23.17) to be satisfied with food on the basis of having eaten enough
senses.comment: See also comments at 23.17.

senses.subdomain: Enjoy, Take Pleasure In, Be Fond of Doing
senses.def: to enjoy something fully and completely, with the implication of satisfying one’s desires
(two different forms of the same base, compare 23.18) to cause someone to be satisfied as the result of food which has been provided in sufficient quantity
senses.comment: It is possible that in Luke 1:53 the reference is to God’s providence in general rather than merely to feeding the hungry.|A strictly literal rendering of ἐμπίμπλημι or ἐμπιπλάω in the sense of ‘to fill with food’ might carry the wrong implication, namely, ‘to stuff with food’ to the point of making someone extremely uncomfortable. It may therefore be important to divide somewhat the complex semantic components of meaning and to translate ‘to cause to eat much and to become happy’ or ‘to cause to eat enough and as a result to be content.’

senses.def: to cause someone to regain strength after a temporary loss
to regain one’s physical strength after a temporary loss of it
senses.comment: It may, however, be impossible to say in some languages ‘his strength came back,’ because this would seem to imply a kind of personification of ‘strength.’ Therefore, it may be necessary to translate this phrase in Acts 9:19 as ‘after he had eaten, he became strong again’ or ‘… he was no longer weak.’

senses.def: to mark an event as being possible in a highly generic sense
senses.comment: In Acts 2:29 the possibility of speaking confidently about David evidently is based upon well-known facts.

senses.def: to be obligatory; to be within the law
a marker of cause or reason, often with the implication of a relevant temporal element

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time which is prior to another point of time, with the possible implication in some contexts of reason or cause
to explain the meaning of something, with the implication that the text in question is difficult or complex
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἐπιλύω ‘to untie, to loose,’ not occurring in the NT) to come to a conclusion concerning a presumably difficult or complex matter
to speak with considerable volume or loudness
pertaining to a state of readiness
pertaining to being devoted to a proper expression of religious beliefs
senses.comment: In a number of languages the concept of ‘living a godly life’ may be best expressed as ‘to live as God would have one live’ or ‘to live like one should who believes in God’ or ‘to always do what God requires.’ In some languages, however, the only equivalent is ‘to live a good life’ or ‘to live always doing good to others.’ The shift from the focus upon religious belief to good living or being good to others results from the fact that in some religious systems there is little or no connection between religious beliefs and moral behavior.

senses.def: a condition of darkness associated with feelings of despair and foreboding
senses.comment: In Hebrews 12:18 γνόφος ‘darkness’ (14.53) and ζόφος may be combined to form a phrase such as ‘fearful darkness’ or ‘darkness that causes fear’ or ‘fear because of darkness.’

senses.subdomain: Regions Below the Surface of the Earth
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: the gloom of darkness) the dark, gloomy nature of hell as a place of punishment
the process of dying
senses.comment: In a number of languages clear distinctions are made in the use of terms for dying on the basis of the manner or circumstances of death. For example, one term may refer to death primarily as the result of old age, while another term may refer to death caused by sickness, and still other terms may be used for death caused by violence. Careful distinctions must be used in determining the choice of terms based on particular contexts.

senses.def: a widespread contagious disease, often associated with divine retribution
(an idiom, literally: to be in death) to be in imminent danger of dying
to cause serious trouble to, with the implication of dire consequences and probably a weakened state
to serve as a priest in the performance of religious rites and duties
senses.comment: In contrast with the prophet who speaks to people on behalf of God, the priest is often defined as one who represents the people before God. In reality, however, the priest is one who is primarily engaged in religious ritual and ceremony in contrast with the prophet, whose primary activity is involved in proclaiming a message. In societies in which there is no organized priesthood and where there are only medicine men or shamans, it has often been possible to translate ἱερουργέω and ἱερατεύω as simply ‘to be God’s shaman.’ Whether such an expression can be used depends very largely upon the connotations associated with shamanism.

senses.def: any creature living in the sea
senses.comment: Though all languages have terms to designate at least certain kinds of fish, there are frequently important distinctions between varieties. In a number of instances distinctions are made between fish which have scales and those which do not (an important distinction in the OT, since it constituted the basis for distinguishing between ‘clean’ or ‘unclean’ varieties). In other languages the distinction may be made between fresh water and salt water fish, while in still other languages a clear distinction is made between edible and inedible fish.|Some languages also distinguish between fish which are still alive in the water and those which have been caught and are in various stages of preparation for being eaten. In Matthew 7:10 ἰχθύς may refer to a piece of fish ready to be eaten.

senses.def: a marker of concession, with the probable implication of an additional component of contrast

senses.subdomain: To Distinguish, To Evaluate, To Judge
senses.def: to judge something to be bad

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to cause someone to suffer ill-treatment
to be distressed, with the implication of being worn out by such an experience
(derivative of κατοικέω ‘to dwell,’ 85.69) a place of dwelling, whether an object or area
a state of dangerous and threatening circumstances
one who exchanges currency, either in terms of different types of currency or different values of the same currency
to come to a conclusion in the process of thinking and thus to be in a position to make a decision
senses.comment: In some languages the process of ‘deciding’ is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to come to the end in one’s thinking’ or ‘to choose in one’s mind’ or ‘the mind sees its goal.’

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: to judge something to be better than something else, and hence, to prefer

senses.subdomain: To Distinguish, To Evaluate, To Judge
senses.def: to make a judgment based upon the correctness or value of something

senses.subdomain: Have an Opinion, Hold a View
senses.def: to hold a view or have an opinion with regard to something
to decide a question of legal right or wrong, and thus determine the innocence or guilt of the accused and assign appropriate punishment or retribution
glosses: to try a case (in the passive to stand trial)
senses.comment: The process of legal judging is often expressed idiomatically. In Africa, one of the standard phrases for judging is ‘to cut a palaver,’ but other expressions in other languages may be ‘to find guilt,’ ‘to point the finger at wrong,’ or ‘to untangle strife.’

senses.def: to judge a person to be guilty and liable to punishment
to rule over people
senses.comment: Though it would be possible to understand κρίνω in Luke 22:30 as meaning ‘to judge’ (see 56.30), the function of the twelve disciples seems to be far greater than that. Furthermore, there seems to be a significant Semitic influence in the meaning of κρίνω, since the corresponding Hebrew term likewise involved far more than merely making judicial decisions.

senses.def: to speak or talk, with the possible implication of more informal usage (though this cannot be clearly and consistently shown from NT contexts)
(an idiom, literally: to speak to the ear) to speak quietly and presumably to a restricted audience
senses.comment: For another treatment of the phrase πρὸς τὸ οὖς, see 28.73.

senses.def: a widespread lack of food over a considerable period of time and resulting in hunger for many people
senses.comment: In a number of languages the only way of talking about a famine is to say ‘many people were very hungry for a long time’ or ‘many people had to go for days without anything to eat.’ It is important to distinguish clearly between a famine and voluntary abstinence from food for the sake of fasting. (See Domain 53H.)

senses.def: the state of being very hungry, presumably for a considerable period of time and as the result of necessity rather than choice (compare νηστεία[a] ‘fasting,’ 53.65)
senses.comment: Terms referring to hunger often distinguish varying degrees of hunger and whether the hunger is by necessity or by choice.

senses.def: a tax collector and one of the twelve apostles, generally regarded as being the same as Λευί 1, 93.231
to cause to be large
senses.comment: It is possible to interpret the large size of the tassels as referring primarily to the length of the tassels and, therefore, to translate as ‘they make their tassels long.’ However, it seems more likely that the reference includes all dimensions.

senses.def: to praise a person in terms of that individuals greatness
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is necessary to restructure a statement such as ‘praising God’s greatness’ as a form of direct discourse, for example, ‘they said, God is indeed great.’

senses.subdomain: Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
senses.def: to show respect to a person on the basis of the importance of such an individual
to feel regret as the result of what one has done
to change one’s mind about something, with the probable implication of regret
(derivative of μισθόομαι ‘to hire,’ 57.172) a person who has been hired to perform a particular service or work
(derivative of Ναζαρέθ ‘Nazareth,’ 93.536) a person who lives in or is a native of Nazareth
senses.comment: Ναζορηνός, Ναζωρηνός, and Ναζωρινός (Mark 10:47, apparatus) are incidental alternative spellings.

senses.def: to regard something as presumably true, but without particular certainty
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ‘to suppose’ or ‘to presume’ is ‘to think somewhat’ or ‘to think perhaps’ or ‘to think a little.’ In some instances the lack of certainty is spelled out clearly as ‘to think, but not with certainty’ or ‘to think, but not to know’ or ‘to think, but not to be sure.’

senses.def: to engage in some activity as a customary practice
senses.comment: This meaning is found as a variant reading only: οὗ ἐνομίζετο προσευχὴ εἶναι ‘where prayer took place’ Acts 16:13 (apparatus). This expression may also be translated as ‘where people customarily prayed.’

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: a piece of linen cloth
senses.comment: In the NT ὀθόνιον occurs only in reference to strips of cloth used in preparing a corpse for burial.

senses.def: the state of being similar to something
any kind of bird, wild or domestic
senses.comment: All languages have at least some terms for birds, but there may be no generic term which identifies birds while excluding all other creatures which fly. For example, in some languages a term which includes all kinds of birds also includes flying insects and bats. However, since in most instances such a term has birds as its primary reference, it can usually be employed in contexts in which birds are more or less readily identified by other expressions in the passage. In other languages generic terms for birds may identify only certain classes of birds, for example, birds of prey, water birds, and birds of the forest.|In the NT occurrences of ὄρνεον, the reference is to unclean birds, either birds of prey or scavengers.

senses.def: (derivative of ὄψιος ‘late,’ 67.76, and used absolutely of ‘late rain’) a rain that comes late in the season, that is to say, in April or May after the normal rains of the winter season have passed
senses.comment: See πρόϊμος ‘early rain’ (14.14) for a discussion of problems involving ‘late rain’ and ‘early rain.’

senses.subdomain: To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately
senses.def: to fail to consider something sufficiently, and as a result, fail to respond appropriately
senses.comment: It may be important to restructure this statement in Acts 6:1 to read ‘because when help was being given out each day, their widows got nothing.’

senses.subdomain: Pass, Cross Over, Go Through, Go Around
senses.def: to move past a reference point
to come to be present at a particular place
to act contrary to established custom or law, with the implication of intent
senses.comment: Languages differ appreciably in the way in which they speak of disobeying or transgressing a law. It is rarely possible to speak of ‘breaking a law,’ since nothing is actually done to the law in the process of transgression, but languages do employ such expressions as ‘to tramp on a law,’ ‘to ridicule a law,’ and ‘to laugh at a law.’ See also discussion at 36.29.

senses.def: to go out of existence

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: to mark the passage of time, with focus upon completion
senses.comment: In Matthew 24:34 it may be important to distinguish carefully between γενεά[a] meaning ‘people’ (11.4) and γενεά[d] meaning ‘time’ (67.144), since this will undoubtedly influence the way in which the temporal reference of παρέρχομαι[e] is represented. If one understands generation in the sense of ‘people,’ then one may translate ‘these people living now will not die until all these things happen.’

senses.def: fifth in a series involving either time, space, or set
(derivative of περισσός[c] ‘abundant,’ 59.51) to be or exist in abundance, with the implication of being considerably more than what would be expected
glosses: to exist in a large quantity
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is extremely difficult to find an equivalent of ‘to abound.’ Moreover, it is not at all easy to find an expression of quantity which seems to go satisfactorily with ‘the sufferings of Christ.’ In some languages the closest equivalent of this expression in 2 Corinthians 1:5 may be ‘for just as we suffer a great deal, even as Christ suffered.’ It would be wrong, however, to use an expression for ‘suffering’ which would suggest vicarious suffering. |The rendering of περισσεύω in Acts 16:5 as ‘to grow’ results from the expression τῷ ἀριθμῷ. In a number of languages the equivalent would be ‘the number of people in the churches increased every day’ or ‘how many believers there were was more and more each day.’

senses.def: to cause something to exist in an abundance
glosses: to provide a great deal of
senses.comment: In some languages, however, it may be very strange to speak of having or receiving an abundance of grace. The closest equivalent for Ephesians 1:7-Ephesians 1:8 may be ‘grace which he caused us to experience abundantly’ or ‘grace which he showed to us in an abundant way.’

senses.def: to have such an abundance as to be more than sufficient
a degree which is considerably in excess of some point on an implied or explicit scale of extent
senses.comment: In Philippians 1:9 it is clear that μᾶλλον καὶ μᾶλλον (see 78.28) serves to emphasize the degree expressed in περισσεύω. The verb περισσεύητε in 1 Thessalonians 4:1 may be regarded as a kind of substitute verb referring to περιπατεῖτε and indicating essentially a matter of degree. This is, of course, further reinforced by μᾶλλον (78.28).

senses.def: to cause an increase in the degree of some experience or state
senses.comment: It would seem that πλεονάσαι and περισσεύσαι in 1 Thessalonians 3:12 simply reinforce the meaning of intense degree. It is assumed that these two expressions are not completely synonymous, but it is difficult to determine precisely how they may contrast. It may simply be that περισσεύσαι is somewhat more emphatic.

senses.def: to experience superior benefit or advantage, implying some type of comparison
senses.comment: In indicating ‘a superior advantage’ it may be necessary to be quite specific about the basis for the comparison. For example, in 1 Corinthians 8:8 it may be necessary to translate as ‘if we do eat, we will be no better off than if we did not eat,’ and in Romans 3:9 one may translate ‘what then; are we decidedly better off than the others are?’

senses.def: pertaining to being wide
senses.comment: In Matthew 7:13 πύλη seems to refer to the gateway (in other words, to the space) rather than to the gate as an object. (See 7.48.)

senses.def: a wide street within a city
a relatively large quantity of objects or events
a relatively large quantity
the upper range of a scale of extent, but probably somewhat less than for μέγας[b], μεγάλως, and μέγεθος (78.2)
senses.comment: In Mark 3:12 πολλά indicates only degree, but it may be rendered in English as ‘sternly’ because part of the meaning of ἐπετίμα may be appropriately transferred to the adverbial attributive so as to express the extent and nature of the warning. In Acts 21:40 the phrase πολλῆς δὲ σιγῆς γενομένης refers to the fact that the crowd became very quiet. πολλῆς clearly indicates the degree of quietness, though in many languages one cannot speak of something being ‘very quiet’; on the contrary, such a state can only be described in terms of the absence of noise, for example, ‘when nobody was saying anything.’

senses.def: the largest number of objects or events possible under the circumstances
a degree which surpasses in some manner a point on an explicit or implicit scale of extent
pertaining to being more appropriate or fitting

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often
senses.def: a number of related points of time

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to a relatively long duration of time
to cut an object in two with a saw
glosses: to cut in two with a saw

senses.def: extension toward a goal, with the probability of some type of implied interaction or reciprocity
extension toward a goal, involving presumed contact and reaction
a position near another location or object, often with the implication of facing toward
a position within an area determined by other objects and distributed among such objects
a marker of an experiencer of an event, with the implication that the participant may then be in some dyadic relation
(with the accusative) a marker of content, particularly when persons are involved and/or the context suggests some type of response being made
senses.comment: For a different interpretation of πρός in Mark 12:12 and Colossians 3:13, see 90.33.

senses.def: a marker of association, often with the implication of interrelationships
a marker of purpose, pointing to the goal of an event or state
a marker of result, with focus upon the end point
a marker of a relation involving correspondence, with the probable implication of some element of reciprocity

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: a marker of a period of time occurring before a subsequent period, and implying anticipation

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often
senses.def: a marker of a point of time, probably implying proximity

senses.subdomain: Up To, As Much As, To the Degree That [Marked Extent of Degree]
senses.def: a degree extending to a particular point as marked by the context
a marker of a relation involving potential interaction
(with the accusative) marking a participant whose viewpoint is relevant to an event
(with the accusative) a marker of opposition, with the probable implication of a reaction or response to a previous event
senses.comment: For another interpretation of πρός in Mark 12:12 and Colossians 3:13, see 90.25.

senses.def: a marker of that which is compared to something else

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to a relatively short period of time, with emphasis upon the temporary nature of the event or state
(an idiom, literally: to kick against the goad) to react against authority in such a way as to cause harm or suffering to oneself
glosses: to hurt oneself by reacting against a person or command

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to a relatively brief extent of time

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: (idiom, literally: to the ear) pertaining to what is known only by those who hear a particular message in private
senses.comment: A phrase such as ‘whatever you hear in secret’ may be rendered as ‘whatever you hear when no one else is listening.’|For another treatment of the phrase πρὸς τὸ οὖς λαλέω, see 33.91.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to speak to the ear) to speak quietly and presumably to a restricted audience
senses.comment: For another treatment of the phrase πρὸς τὸ οὖς, see 28.73.

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: pertaining to a point of time preceding another point of time, but with a relatively short interval
senses.comment: For languages which do not have an adverb meaning ‘recently,’ one can always introduce an equivalent approximate statement in Acts 18:2, for example, ‘he met a Jew who only a few days before had come from Italy.’ One cannot be certain as to the interval of time, but a phrase such as ‘a few days before’ can be a satisfactory equivalent.

senses.def: doors or gates used to close off entranceways
senses.comment: πύλη and πυλών[a] may refer to house doors and gates or to large doors and gates such as were used in a palace, temple, or in a city wall.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: gates of Hades) death as an impersonal supernatural power
senses.comment: Some scholars, however, understand πύλαι ᾅδου to mean Satanic powers of evil.

senses.def: a son of Σίμων[d] of Cyrene
a person greeted in Romans 16:13
to cause a fire to be extinguished
senses.comment: ‘To put out fierce fires’ may be expressed as ‘to cause fierce fires no longer to burn’ or ‘to make large fires stop burning.’ In order to speak of ‘fierce fires’ it may be necessary in some languages to speak of ‘large, hot fires.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σβέννυμι[a] ‘to extinguish a fire,’ 14.70) to cause a fervent activity to cease
senses.comment: Though the particular activity of the Spirit is not overtly indicated in the context of 1 Thessalonians 5:19, the book as a whole contains sufficient reference to the activity of the Spirit so as to indicate what is involved.

senses.def: to cease burning, either because of lack of material to be burned or because the fire has been forcibly extinguished
senses.comment: The expression ‘our lamps are going out’ may be rendered as ‘our lamps will soon not be burning’ or ‘our lamps will burn only a little bit more.’ It may, however, be misleading to speak of ‘lamps burning’ (see discussion in 14.65), and accordingly, it may be much better to translate ‘our lamps will show light only a little bit more’ or ‘the oil in our lamps will burn only a little bit more.’

senses.def: a Jewish high priest
to cause a spot or stain upon something
to bring together into a unit
glosses: to cause to be a unit

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of συμβιβάζω[a] ‘to bring together, to unite, to combine,’ 63.5) to come to a solution or a decision, implying a process of putting together different aspects of related information
to cause something to be known as certain and therefore dependable
senses.comment: In a number of languages one may express certainty by a negative phrase, for example, ‘so that no one could ever doubt.’ In other instances, an idiomatic expression may be used, for example, ‘with heavy words’ or ‘with words that speak to the heart’ or ‘with words that are like rocks.’

senses.def: to advise by giving instructions
to become larger together with, in the sense of growing in essentially the same area and at the same time (compare συμφύομαι, 23.193)
(derivative of Συροφοινικία ‘Syro-Phoenicia,’ not occurring in the NT) a woman who is a native of Syro-Phoenicia
senses.comment: See also discussion at 10.1.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to having the attitude of humility
to cause a state to continue
senses.comment: In 1 Corinthians 7:37 the reference to ‘girl’ may be either a man’s daughter or a man’s fiancée. Because of the ambiguity of this statement in 1 Corinthians 7:37 and in view of the cultural complications involved, especially because of differences of customs in different parts of the world, it is important that translators add a note at this point explaining the difference of interpretation and some of the cultural implications.

senses.def: to continue to hold in custody
senses.comment: The act of holding someone in custody or guarding an individual may be expressed as ‘standing guard to see that someone will not escape’ or ‘watching carefully so that one cannot run off’ or ‘tying someone up so that he cannot leave.’

senses.def: to continue to obey orders or commandments
the process of turning, with the implication of variation and change
senses.comment: It is difficult to know precisely the significance of the phrase τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα. It probably had a technical sense which has been lost, but clearly it is parallel in meaning to παραλλαγή ‘change, alteration’ (58.44). In some languages it may be best to translate this expression in James 1:17 as ‘in whom there is no change or variation.’

senses.def: (derivative of ὑπάρχω[d] ‘to belong to,’ 57.2) that which constitutes someone’s possession
to sail or move along beside some object which provides a degree of protection or shelter
glosses: to sail under the shelter of

senses.def: to move toward and to arrive at a point
to come/go prior to some other event, normally one involving a similar type of movement
senses.comment: Though the movement referred to by φθάνω[b] and προέρχομαι[c] may involve movement which is spacially ahead of someone else, nevertheless the focus of meaning is not a spacial relationship but a temporal one.

senses.def: to attain or arrive at a particular state
senses.comment: Though grammatically it is the law which is not attained in Romans 9:31, semantically it is, of course, the state of righteousness which was the ultimate goal, and hence it was this particular state which was not attained.

senses.def: to happen to someone prior to a particular point in time
a Christian of Corinth
a state of joy and gladness
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘joy’ is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘my heart is dancing’ or ‘my heart shouts because I am happy.’

senses.def: that which is the cause of joy or gladness

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: one who is identified as a believer in and follower of Christ
to produce a howling or roaring sound, typically of wolves, but also applicable to lions
senses.comment: For languages spoken by people who are acquainted with the behavior of lions in the wild, there should be no difficulty in obtaining a specific term applicable to lions. In the case of other languages, one can often use a more generic expression such as ‘to make a great noise.’
